extracted.intended_audience: mathematics department faculty and assessment coordinators designing/operating senior comprehensives and core assessments for undergraduate mathematics majors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars for designing, administering, and scoring senior comprehensive examinations and core assessment instruments (written and oral, individual and team) in undergraduate mathematics; includes item selection, grading rubrics, logistics, and uses of results to drive curricular change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essay component requirements (Wabash)
rubrics_metrics.description: "write an essay which includes definitions of appropriate terms, relevant examples and counter-examples, statements of several important theorems, and the proof in detail (including proofs of lemmas used) of at least one of these theorems."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students are given a short list of potential topics in advance and are encouraged to prepare these essays (even consult faculty) but must write the essay without notes on exam day. Examiners look for the student's ability to choose appropriate examples and theorems, to explain them, and to put this all together into a coherent whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-essay (problem) design criteria (Wabash)
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems should be "typical course test problems" that "cover the main points of the courses" and are "not supposed to require memorization of too much information or otherwise be too obscure; rather, they should cover the main points of the courses."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whoever taught a given course in the last two years submits problems (three each); an exam committee selects from submissions aiming for a balance of easy and difficult problems and ensuring the second day's advanced topics allow each student to choose problems from courses he has studied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance of aids to emphasize conceptual understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy example: "we decided that we were interested in how well students understand calculus concepts, not in how well they remembered formulas they had learned three years earlier. So we allowed them to bring texts or a sheet of formulas to the first day’s exam."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision about permits (texts, formula sheets, calculators) may change year-to-year to align with assessment priorities (conceptual understanding vs. recall).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymous identification and double-grading procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: "Students are given identification numbers (the correspondence between names and ID numbers is sealed until the written exams have been graded and grades decided on), and all questions are double-graded, with the department sharing equally the job of grading."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When there is substantial disagreement between graders of a given question, graders review all papers answering that question and regrade that question together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral examination structure and scope (Wabash)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The oral is a 50-minute exam with each student examined by three faculty members, one from the major, one from the minor, and one at-large."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oral questions often probe philosophical understanding and the ability to explain mathematics to non-specialists (e.g., "is mathematics a science or an art?" or "explain the idea of the derivative" to a classics professor). The oral also assesses minors and provides information different from the written part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighting and separate-passing requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: "The college requires that the oral component comprise 1/4 of the grade, but that, to pass the comprehensive examination, students must pass both the oral and written parts separately."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Departments may set numerical thresholds for passing (example: failing below 60% overall on written triggers failing status) and require retakes at specified times; passing rules affect student behavior and departmental remediation policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling and retake logistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Exams scheduled to allow timely retakes: written exams moved to first days of spring semester so grades are turned in by spring break and failing students can retake in April to still graduate with their class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing choices trade off student class time and fairness in retake opportunity; historical changes cited as rationale for current schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract major advising to enable early remediation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Each student signs a contract with the department describing what direction he plans his major to take... The contract is signed before registration for the second semester of the sophomore year... Each contract has some flexibility..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to have students work with the department earlier so problems (e.g., poor preparation) can be addressed before senior year; contracts can be changed by petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using exam findings to drive curricular change
rubrics_metrics.description: Departments should analyze patterns of student success and weaknesses on comprehensives and adapt requirements/courses accordingly (examples given: requiring abstract algebra and real variables, introducing theorem-based linear algebra, calculus reform, more active learning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment results are used to identify curricular gaps and to design programmatic reforms (developmental strands, course goals) rather than only isolated course fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint written comprehensive format (team-based, Franklin College)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Students are divided into teams of 3–5. They are given a week to complete the test... Tests consist of four to five open-ended questions, and involve modeling, developing conjectures and writing proofs, and use of library and electronic information resources. Any available mathematical software is allowed. The team distributes the workload... and is responsible for submitting one answer to each question."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The team-based, take-home, open-resource format assesses modeling, collaboration, information use, and the experiment-conjecture-proof process rather than timed individual recall.

rubrics_metrics.name: External author/grader for joint written exam
rubrics_metrics.description: "We have a colleague from another college or university who is familiar with our environment write and grade the joint written comprehensive exam for a small stipend."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using an external reviewer provides variety in questions, an outside perspective, and reduces internal workload; logistical challenges include funding and identifying willing colleagues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation and weighting of multiple practicum components
rubrics_metrics.description: "Results from each of the components of the senior comprehensive practicum (the oral examination, the joint written examination, and the MFAT) are converted into a grade. These grades are assigned a numerical value and averaged on a weighted basis for a grade on the entire practicum... The oral examination is weighted slightly more than the other two..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The combined practicum grade appears on the transcript (no impact on GPA in example) and is part of senior seminar grading; component weighting reflects perceived breadth/depth and complements of instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint written exam assessment focus areas (findings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings identify specific assessment targets: need for more focus on modeling; students have difficulty approaching modeling problems and communicating assumptions and solutions; room for improvement in use of information resources; strengths in use of technology and collaborative development of solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Results should inform curriculum additions (e.g., modeling requirement or courses) and programmatic emphasis on modeling and information literacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core-assessment learning targets (Ball State)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectations for core courses: "the ability to link and integrate concepts, the ability to compare and contrast within a conceptual framework, the ability to analyze situations, the ability to conjecture and test hypotheses, formation of reasoning patterns, and the gaining of insights useful in problem solving."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment instruments should maximize focus on student cognitive activity and growth attributable to concept exposure, independent of instructor variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item selection criteria and formats (Ball State)
rubrics_metrics.description: A combined pool of items used various formats: true/false, multiple choice, and free response. Selection criteria: there should be a mix of problem formats, and approximately half of the questions should be nonstandard (not typically used on in-class examinations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonstandard questions include tasks like finding errors in sample work, extending beyond typical cases, tying together related ideas, and asking for justified examples or paragraph discussions. Parts were designed to take ~90 minutes each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration conditions to elicit authentic responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Students who had completed appropriate core components were encouraged to participate on a voluntary basis during an evening session; students were not instructed to study or prepare for the activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encouraging complete written responses and a low-pressure voluntary environment produced authentic, considered responses in the pilot administrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring rubric (Ball State Table 1: 3/2/1/0)
rubrics_metrics.description: Score 3: "Conceptual understanding apparent; consistent notation, with only an occasional error; logical formulation; complete or near-complete solution/response." Score 2: "Conceptual understanding only adequate; careless mathematical errors present (algebra, arithmetic, for example); some logical steps lacking; incomplete solution/response." Score 1: "Conceptual understanding not adequate; procedural errors; logical or relational steps missing; poor response or no response to the question posed." Score 0: "Does not attempt problem or conceptual understanding totally lacking."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rubric guided independent scoring of responses; differences in interpretation were resolved jointly by scorers. (Authors note they did not formally address inter-rater reliability or statistical item analysis in the pilot.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring process and reviewer reconciliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses were evaluated independently by investigators using a scoring rubric; "differences in interpretation were resolved jointly through discussion and additional consideration of the responses."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit process for reconciling scores is recommended; the example admits lack of formal inter-rater reliability measurement or item analysis and flags these as unaddressed in the pilot.
